You've been here twenty minutes. Two men entered with your name on their faces but no Brandt signet. Nothing yet.

Through the glass, a long black sedan crawls along the curb. Slow. Too slow. The kind of vehicle that doesn't belong at a dockside bar.

content: I walk over to the man in the grey coat, sit down and ask what cargo he needs moving and where to.

He goes rigid the moment your shadow falls across his glass. One hand slides under the table. Then he sees your face and relaxes, almost.

"Captain Venn." Not a question. "I was hoping you'd come to me. Saves us both the small talk." He taps a data-chip on the bar top. "I'm Pell. Independent logistics. I need a cargo run out of here to Varo Station, via Kessel. Standard haul, sealed containers, no manifest I can share until we're in transit."

He checks the door behind you. "Pays fifty thousand. Up front. Half now, half on delivery. I know what you owe Brandt. I also know he doesn't like me breathing."

His eyes are flat, tired, the look of a man who's been running this play before. "I don't ask what's in the containers. You don't ask what they are. Deal?"

The chip gleams under the bar's fluorescent hum. Behind him, the rain still streaks the glass.

content: Fine. 12,000 credits for the crates to Regina, half up front. I shake on it and ask his name.

Pell's hand, which was reaching for the chip, stops mid-air.

"Regina." He says the word like it tastes bad. "Captain, I didn't offer you a bus route." He pulls the chip back under his sleeve. "Fifty thousand. Varo via Kessel. That's the job. You haul what I give you, where I give you, and you don't lowball me in a dockside bar like I'm some port-side tinker selling fuel injectors."

He leans forward. "And you want *my* name. After trying to cut me to a quarter. That's either very brave or very stupid, and I can't tell which, and it doesn't much matter."

He stands. His chair scrapes. "Walk away, Captain. There'll be other work. Most of it won't pay fifty thousand, and most of it won't ask you to look at the stars and not think about what's in them."

He pauses at the bar's edge, back still half-turned.

"…But the door's behind you. Rain's not going to stop."

The bartender's jaw clicks. The grey coat dissolves into the back-room crowd.

content: I head back to the Wandering Star and tell Dex and Mira we have a job. Let's load the crates and lift off.

The walk back to the Wandering Star takes six minutes through the rain. Dex is under the port thruster, greased to the elbow. Mira's on the cockpit rail, smoking something thin.

"Job," you announce.

Dex looks up. "Which job?"

"Grey coat. Pell. Varo run. Fifty grand."

Mira snuffs her smoke. "You shook on it?"

The question hangs. You did reach. He pulled back. He *left.*

Dex wipes his hands on a rag. "No chip. No manifest. No crates in the bay." He gestures at the empty hold hatch behind him. "There's nothing to load, Kara. You're talking to yourself."

Mira slides off the rail. "And fifty thousand is exactly four thousand more than the Brandt debt. You think a 'Pell' hands that over in a bar and calls it a quarter-price job? You think he *walked away* and the deal still stands?"

Dex shrugs. "I can start the engines. Nowhere to go."

The rain hammers the hull. The bar's neon bleeds through the mist behind you.

content: Once we're clear of Ruie we jump for Regina.

Mira's hand stops on the nav console. "Regina." She types it in. The system returns: *NO ENTRY. STAR NOT IN MARCHES CHART.*

"You can't jump there, Kara. It's not in our nav plot. Could be a backwater in the Reach, could be a name you made up to sound smart in a bar. Either way, I need a bearing and a star number, and I don't have either."

Dex, from the engine deck, calls up: "Even if you did, we've got fuel for one jump, maybe two. And we've got *nothing* in the hold. You're burning credits to go nowhere with no cargo and no deal." He pauses. "Also, Brandt's people don't care where the ship is. They care where *you* are. Jumping doesn't fix the debt. It just makes us harder to find, and harder to find a job."

Mira turns from the console. "So. We sit here. Or we go back to that bar. Or you tell me you actually know a star called Regina and where the hell it is, and I'll try to plot it."

The rain hasn't let up.

content: Fine, forget Regina. Mira, plot a jump to Efate. We'll look for honest cargo there. Lift off and jump.

Mira plots Efate without complaint. One jump. Fuel's fine. She runs the pre-flight checklist while Dex cycles the drive.

content: When we arrive at Efate, I take the shuttle down to the startown and go looking for the freight brokers' hall.

The shuttle drops through cloud layer and out. Efate's startown is a sprawl of corrugated sheds and a single concrete port ring, half of it still concrete. No neon. No rain. Just dusty wind and the smell of cut grass and diesel.

The freight brokers' hall is a low building with a tin roof that rattles. Inside, it's a long counter under hanging bulbs, six brokers hunched over terminals, a corkboard of handwritten manifests, and the smell of cheap coffee that's been sitting since morning.

A broker with a shaved head and a Marches ID clipped to her shirt looks up. "Wandering Star. Name's in the port registry. You're new here." She taps the counter. "Crate runs, ore, livestock, the usual. Or you're early for the survey team's supply drop." She points at a name on the board: **KELVIN-ORR LOGISTICS — 200 T, MINE SHAFT 7 TO ORBIT, 800 C/T, CARGO: RAW ORE, HAZARD: NONE, DEADLINE: 12 DAYS.**

She shrugs. "Best thing on the board. Everyone else is running shuttles or moving crates of rice."

The other brokers don't look up.

content: I ask the broker whether she's heard of a skinny man in a grey coat running sealed cargo out to the Kessel route. And whether anyone here works for the loan shark I owe money to.

The broker's jaw tightens, just slightly.

"Grey coat, skinny. Yeah, we've got a Pell running sealed containers up the Kessel lane. Twice a month, maybe. Doesn't dock here. Goes direct to the transfer point." She shrugs. "Hearsay. I don't do his paperwork."

She leans forward an inch. "The other question, though." Her voice drops. "You're asking about Brandt in a *town* like this, in front of six other people." She glances down the counter at the other brokers, who haven't looked up, but who *will* hear.

"Nobody here works for him. Efate's too small, too polite, too far from Ruie's jurisdiction to keep a loan shark's book open. But people *talk* about Brandt. You've announced yourself to anyone with ears." She taps the counter twice. "If his people were already watching this system, you just made their job easier. If they weren't, now you've created a reason for them to look."

content: I thank the broker, and ask what honest cargo she has going anywhere spinward.

The broker nods, satisfied you're moving past Brandt. "Spinward, you mean toward the Marches proper. So, *everywhere* on my board, basically."

She turns back to the corkboard and pulls off three cards.

**One:** The ore run. Kelvin-Orr. 200 tonnes, mine shaft to orbit. 800 credits per tonne. Twelve days. Boring. Safe. "This is the one I'd take if I had a ship and a debt."

**Two:** A livestock haul. Sixty head of breeding goats from a rural port to a processing barge in orbit. 3,200 credits flat. Five days. "Smells like a barn for a week. The goats aren't happy about it either."

**Three:** A survey team needs a ride and a bunk. Two scientists, one pilot, four days to a mapping station in the outer system. 1,500 credits flat. "They'll pay you in *gratitude* and a stamped manifest you can't sell. But you'll have fuel topped and a good story."

"Ore's the real money. The rest is filler between runs."

content: Ore run sounds right. I take the Kelvin-Orr job and ask when the ore will be ready to load.

The broker nods, satisfied. She keys a code into her terminal and a small printer beside the counter grinds out a stamped manifest.

"Mine shaft seven, south face of the continent. Ground transport gets the ore up to the port ring in about ninety minutes. Your shuttle can't get there, but the *Star* can dock at the orbital lift terminal." She hands you the manifest. "Pickup window's tomorrow, 0600 to 0900. You'll need to file a berth request before midnight."

She glances at the manifest, then at you.

"Two hundred tonnes. That's your full hold capacity, right? Battered trader, yes. But you'll need to confirm the *Star's* structural cert is current for that weight. If it's expired, I can only sign you up for one-fifty tonnes and the rate drops to seven-fifty."

She's watching your face for the flinch.

content: I ask her if she knows anyone on Efate who might front a bit of credit against the ore contract.

The broker considers this. She taps her chin with a stained finger.

"Credit against a contract. You want a front." She glances toward the back of the hall, where a narrow door reads **EFATE TRADING CO. — ADVANCES & PROVISIONS.**

"Old Man Teske runs that office. He fronts against contracts, fuel, parts. Not a bank. Not a shark. He's been doing it thirty years, mostly for miners and ranchers who need forty-eight hours of working capital." She shrugs. "He'll look at the Kelvin-Orr manifest, check your ship's cert, check your credit record. If it all squares, he'll front you maybe ten, fifteen thousand against delivery. Interest's ugly. Three, four percent on the nose. He won't do twenty. He'll know you need it badly, and he'll *know*."

She leans back.

"He's in the back office. I can introduce you. Or you can walk in and look scared, which he'll also notice."

A small, honest smile. "I'd go in calm. He hates people who ask nicely."

content: Deal. I head back up to the Wandering Star to prep for loading.

You take the mag-rail back to the dock ring. The *Wandering Star* hangs on its mooring clamps, hull pitted and paint peeling, looking like a barnacle with ambitions.

Dex is already at the cargo bay, running a diagnostic on the structural lacing. He looks up, grease on his forearms.

"Manifest on the board. Two hundred tonnes of raw ore. I'm pulling the structural cert right now." He taps the screen. "Bad news. The aft frame rating is at ninety-one percent. We're under the two-oh threshold."

Mira leans against the bulkhead, arms crossed. "So we're capped at one-fifty tonnes? Broker said the rate drops to seven-fifty."

Dex runs the numbers aloud. "One-fifty at seven-fifty. Twelve days. Nine thousand, twelve hundred."

Mira looks at you. "Against forty thousand owed."

Dex is already pulling up the frame schematic. "If I re-sequence the load distribution, shift three tonnes to the port hardpoint, I can *maybe* squeeze in a couple more. But I'd have to be in the aft bay all night. And if I'm wrong, we crack a frame on the way to orbit."

He looks at you. "Your call, Captain."
